svg.text: WOTS+: the basic structure
What is signed: a digit D, taken as an integer with 0 ≤ D ≤ w − 1
Key generation
1. pick one random start per chain s₀, s₁, …, s₇
2. hash each one w − 1 times pₖ = Hʷ⁻¹(sₖ)
public key: p₀, p₁, …, p₇
secret key: s₀, s₁, …, s₇
(indices shown at w = 8)
Chain structure, drawn at w = 8
chain 0
chain 1
chain 7
each chain is w − 1 = 7 hashes long; pₖ = Hʷ⁻¹(sₖ)
Signing
To sign the digit D, with 0 ≤ D ≤ w − 1:
on chain 0, the signature element is σ₀ = Hᴰ(s₀)
on chain 1, the checksum element is σ₁ = Hʷ⁻¹⁻ᴰ(s₁)
Example: w = 8, D = 2
chain 0 (signs D = 2)
σ₀
chain 1 (signs w − 1 − D = 5)
σ₁
signature (σ₀, σ₁) = (H²(s₀), H⁵(s₁))
Verification
The verifier holds (σ₀, σ₁) and the digit D:
compute p′₀ = Hʷ⁻¹⁻ᴰ(σ₀)
compute p′₁ = Hᴰ(σ₁)
accept iff p′₀ = p₀ and p′₁ = p₁
Example: w = 8, D = 2
chain 0: from σ₀ at 2, walk 5 more → p′₀
chain 1: from σ₁ at 5, walk 2 more → p′₁
both hold, so the signature is valid
Why a checksum chain is needed
With only the message chain, an adversary holding σ₀ = Hᴰ(s₀) can hash it further
to Hᴰ⁺¹(s₀), Hᴰ⁺²(s₀), … and so forge every larger digit.
Adding σ₁ = Hʷ⁻¹⁻ᴰ(s₁) reverses that: forging D′ > D requires walking chain 1
backwards from Hʷ⁻¹⁻ᴰ(s₁) to Hʷ⁻¹⁻ᴰ′(s₁), which is inverting the hash.
In general
A digest is split into several digits, each
signed on its own chain, and the checksum
of all of them gets chains of its own.
chains = ⌈ lg n / lg w ⌉ + checksum chains
SHRINCS uses this twice, differently.
WOTS-TW keeps the checksum: 32 message chains and 3 checksum chains at w = 16, inside the stateless fallback.
WOTS+C drops it, constraining the 32 indexes to sum to 240 instead, which is what fixes the verifier's work.
